docs.title: go-tls-srp
docs.text:
go-tls-srp is a Go library for TLS-SRP: TLS 1.2 with the Secure Remote Password key exchange of RFC 5054. Its package srptls has a client and a server. The client proves that it knows a password. The server stores only a verifier derived from the password, needs no certificate and proves to the client that it holds the verifier.

Go's crypto/tls has no SRP. This module is a trimmed copy of crypto/tls from Go 1.27.2 that keeps only the SRP handshake, so its API follows crypto/tls: a Config, a Conn that implements net.Conn, Client, Server, Listen and ConnectionState. It is written for systems that already use TLS-SRP, such as EST enrollment (RFC 7030) with certificate-less mutual authentication.

go get github.com/misiektoja/go-tls-srp

The module needs Go 1.27.3 or newer. It depends on filippo.io/bigmod for the SRP arithmetic and on golang.org/x/crypto/cryptobyte for message parsing. The package name differs from the module path, so import it with a name:

import srptls "github.com/misiektoja/go-tls-srp"

  • go-acme-server: an embeddable ACME server library for Go (RFC 8555)

  • go-pki-est: a Go library for Enrollment over Secure Transport (EST, RFC 7030) with a client and a server

docs.title: Where the code comes from
docs.text:
The package is a trimmed copy of crypto/tls from Go 1.27.2. It keeps the record layer, the TLS 1.2 key schedule and the handshake message encoding. It replaces the key exchange with SRP. Code that SRP does not use is removed: TLS 1.3, session resumption, certificates, ALPN and QUIC.

File Content conn.go Conn, the record layer, CBC record protection, Handshake, Read, Write and Close common.go Config, ConnectionState, ClientHelloInfo and the sentinel errors tls.go Client, Server, Listen and NewListener handshake_server.go The server handshake handshake_client.go The client handshake, which follows the TLS 1.2 part of Go's client handshake_messages.go Encoding and parsing of the handshake messages, including the SRP structures cipher_suites.go The three SRP cipher suites prf.go The TLS 1.2 PRF, the master secret, Extended Master Secret and exported keying material alert.go TLS alerts srp.go Groups, verifiers, SimulatedVerifier and the SRP computations groups_rfc5054.go The primes and generators of RFC 5054, Appendix A

alert.go, cipher_suites.go, common.go, conn.go, handshake_messages.go, handshake_server.go, prf.go and tls.go are tracked against the same files in newer Go releases, so that fixes to Go's TLS code are ported. Development describes the check.

The SRP arithmetic uses filippo.io/bigmod, the constant-time modular arithmetic of the Go standard library exported as a module. Messages are parsed with golang.org/x/crypto/cryptobyte, as in crypto/tls.

docs.title: The handshake
docs.text:
Every connection runs a full TLS 1.2 handshake with the SRP key exchange of RFC 5054, Section 2.2. There is no certificate message and no signature.

sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant S as Server
    C->>S: ClientHello with the username in the srp extension
    Note over S: picks a cipher suite, calls GetVerifier
    S->>C: ServerHello
    S->>C: ServerKeyExchange with N, g, salt and B
    S->>C: ServerHelloDone
    Note over C: checks the group and B, computes A and the premaster secret
    C->>S: ClientKeyExchange with A
    C->>S: ChangeCipherSpec and Finished
    Note over S: checks A, computes the premaster secret, verifies the Finished message
    S->>C: ChangeCipherSpec and Finished
    Note over C: verifies the Finished message

The server computes B = k*v + g^b mod N from the stored verifier v. The client computes the premaster secret from the password and the server from the verifier (RFC 5054, Section 2.6). Both arrive at the same value only when the verifier was made from the password the client used. Nothing else in the handshake checks the password.

With a wrong password the two sides derive different keys. The server cannot decrypt the client's Finished message and sends a bad_record_mac alert, which the client reports as a wrong password. A server that does not hold the verifier cannot produce a Finished message the client can decrypt, so the client ends the handshake with its own bad_record_mac alert. That is how the client authenticates the server without a certificate.

The random exponents a and b are 384 bits long. RFC 5054 requires that A and B are not zero modulo N. The package also refuses values that are not below N or that give u = 0. A failed check ends the handshake with an illegal_parameter alert.

docs.title: When the handshake runs
docs.text:
The handshake runs when Handshake or HandshakeContext is called or on the first Read or Write. It runs once. A failed handshake stores its error and every later call to Handshake, Read and Write returns it. After a canceled HandshakeContext the stored error is the one from the closed connection, not the context error.

On the server, GetVerifier is called once per handshake, after the cipher suite is chosen and before any SRP computation. Its ClientHelloInfo.Context is canceled when the handshake ends.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: This page creates a verifier, starts a server and signs in to it with a client in one program. The code is Example in example_test.go, which go test runs and checks against its output.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
go get github.com/misiektoja/go-tls-srp

The module needs Go 1.27.3 or newer.

docs.title: Create a verifier
docs.text:
The server never sees the password. It stores a verifier made from the username, the password, a random salt and one of the RFC 5054 groups:

group, err := srptls.GroupByBits(3072)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
salt, err := srptls.NewSalt(rand.Reader)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
stored, err := srptls.NewVerifier(group, []byte("device-1"), []byte("secret"), salt)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

A real server creates the verifier once when the user is enrolled. It stores the group size, the salt and the value. Verifiers and groups describes what to store and how to import verifiers made by OpenSSL.

docs.title: Start the server
docs.text:
Config.GetVerifier returns the stored verifier for the username in the ClientHello. Listen returns a net.Listener whose connections are *srptls.Conn:

l, err := srptls.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0", &srptls.Config{
    GetVerifier: func(info *srptls.ClientHelloInfo) (*srptls.Verifier, error) {
        if info.Username == "device-1" {
            return stored, nil
        }
        return nil, srptls.ErrUnknownUsername
    },
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

go func() {
    c, err := l.Accept()
    if err != nil {
        return
    }
    defer c.Close()
    // The library sets no handshake deadline.
    c.SetDeadline(time.Now().Add(10 * time.Second))
    conn := c.(*srptls.Conn)
    if err := conn.Handshake(); err != nil {
        log.Print(err)
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintf(conn, "hello %s\n", conn.ConnectionState().SRPUsername)
}()

Returning ErrUnknownUsername tells the client that the username does not exist. Unknown usernames and refusals shows how to hide that instead.

docs.title: Connect a client
docs.text:
Client wraps a connection you dialed. The handshake checks the server's group and its Finished message, so it succeeds only when the server holds the verifier of this username and password:

raw, err := net.DialTimeout("tcp", l.Addr().String(), 10*time.Second)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
conn := srptls.Client(raw, &srptls.Config{
    Username:   "device-1",
    Password:   "secret",
    ServerName: "localhost",
})
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
err = conn.HandshakeContext(ctx)
cancel()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

greeting, err := bufio.NewReader(conn).ReadString('\n')
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
state := conn.ConnectionState()
fmt.Print(greeting)
fmt.Println(srptls.CipherSuiteName(state.CipherSuite))
fmt.Println("extended master secret:", state.ExtendedMasterSecret)
fmt.Println("tls-unique bytes:", len(state.TLSUnique))
conn.Close()

The program prints:

hello device-1
TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA
extended master secret: true
tls-unique bytes: 12

To run it from a checkout of the repository:

go test -run '^Example$' -v .

docs.title: What to change for production
docs.text:
• Store verifiers instead of passwords and protect them like password hashes. Whoever reads a verifier can test password guesses offline and can pose as the server to that user (RFC 5054, Section 3.3).
  • Decide how to answer unknown usernames. SimulatedVerifier makes them fail like a wrong password, as Unknown usernames and refusals describes.
  • Set a deadline on every accepted connection before its handshake and limit the connections a client can open. The library sets no handshake deadline. See Running a server.
  • Limit password guessing by counting failed handshakes and refusing clients over the limit in GetVerifier. See Limiting password guessing.
  • With net/http, use the setup on Running a server and Connecting as a client, because Request.TLS and Response.TLS stay nil for these connections.

docs.title: TLS 1.2 only
docs.text: SRP has cipher suites only up to TLS 1.2, so the package neither offers nor negotiates TLS 1.3. It refuses TLS 1.0 and 1.1. A peer that cannot do TLS 1.2 cannot connect.

docs.title: Only the RFC 5054 groups
docs.text: The package has no way to define a group beyond the seven of RFC 5054, Appendix A. A verifier made in another group cannot be used. The client refuses a server that sends one.

docs.title: Only the certificate-less SRP cipher suites
docs.text: The SRP_SHA_RSA and SRP_SHA_DSS cipher suites, in which the server also signs with a certificate, are not implemented. All three supported suites use CBC with HMAC-SHA1 and the partial Lucky13 countermeasures of crypto/tls.

docs.title: No session resumption
docs.text: There are no session IDs and no session tickets. Every connection runs a full handshake with its modular exponentiations, which matters for clients that open many short connections.

docs.title: No renegotiation
docs.text: Neither side renegotiates. The server answers any handshake message after the handshake with an unexpected_message alert. The client answers a HelloRequest with a no_renegotiation warning, after which the connection can no longer be written to.

docs.title: No SASLprep
docs.text: RFC 5054, Section 2.3 asks for usernames and passwords to be prepared with SASLprep. The package hashes them as given, as OpenSSL does. Peers that apply SASLprep compute different verifiers for strings that SASLprep changes.

docs.title: The username is sent in the clear
docs.text: The client sends the username in the ClientHello without protection. RFC 5054 suggests renegotiating an SRP handshake inside a first, protected one to hide it, which this package cannot do because it does not renegotiate.

docs.title: Not crypto/tls
docs.text: *srptls.Conn is not a *tls.Conn. Code that type-asserts *tls.Conn, such as net/http when it fills Request.TLS and Response.TLS, does not see these connections as TLS. There is also no ALPN, so HTTP/2 cannot be negotiated.

docs.title: No deadline or rate limit
docs.text: The library sets no handshake deadline, no connection limit and no limit on failed sign-ins. The caller provides them, as the Security model describes.

docs.title: Other features
docs.text: Certificates, ALPN, encrypt-then-MAC, compression, QUIC and Encrypted Client Hello are not implemented.

docs.title: Support matrix
docs.text: What the client and the server implement. Known limitations explains the gaps.

docs.title: Protocol versions
docs.text:
Version Client Server TLS 1.2 Offered, the only version Negotiated TLS 1.3 Not offered Not negotiated. A client that offers TLS 1.2 as well gets TLS 1.2 TLS 1.0 and 1.1 Not offered. A server that selects another version than TLS 1.2 gets a protocol_version alert Refused with a protocol_version alert

RFC 5054 defines SRP cipher suites only up to TLS 1.2, so there is nothing to negotiate in TLS 1.3. The server decides on the version field of the ClientHello and ignores supported_versions.

docs.title: Cipher suites
docs.text:
Cipher suite ID Default TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA 0xC020 Yes, first TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA 0xC01D Yes, second TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA 0xC01A No, only when listed in Config.CipherSuites

The SRP_SHA_RSA and SRP_SHA_DSS suites of RFC 5054, which also sign with a server certificate, are not implemented. Cipher suites describes the selection rules.

docs.title: SRP groups
docs.text:
Both sides use only the seven groups of RFC 5054, Appendix A.

Prime size in bits Generator Client default 1024 2 Refused unless Config.MinGroupBits allows it 1536 2 Refused unless Config.MinGroupBits allows it 2048 2 Accepted 3072 5 Accepted 4096 5 Accepted 6144 5 Accepted 8192 19 Accepted

The server sends the group of the verifier that GetVerifier returns. The client refuses any other prime or generator with an insufficient_security alert. See Verifiers and groups.

docs.title: Extensions
docs.text:
Extension Client Server srp (RFC 5054, Section 2.8.1) Sends Config.Username Required. A ClientHello without it fails with unknown_psk_identity server_name (RFC 6066, Section 3) Sends Config.ServerName without a trailing dot. Sends nothing for an empty name or an IP address Reads the host name, passes it to GetVerifier and acknowledges it. Refuses a name with a trailing dot or two host names extended_master_secret (RFC 7627) Always offered. A server without it is accepted Used whenever the client offers it renegotiation_info (RFC 5746) Sends the empty extension instead of the signaling cipher suite Accepts the extension or the signaling cipher suite and answers with the empty extension Any other A server that answers with an extension the client did not send fails with unsupported_extension Ignored

A ClientHello that repeats an extension fails to parse and gets a decode_error alert.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Feature Status Mutual authentication with a password and a verifier Supported tls-unique channel binding (RFC 5929) ConnectionState.TLSUnique on both sides Keying material exporters (RFC 5705) ConnectionState.ExportKeyingMaterial, only with Extended Master Secret NSS key log for debugging Config.KeyLogWriter on both sides Renegotiation Refused. See Known limitations Session resumption and tickets Not implemented. Every handshake is a full handshake Certificates Not implemented ALPN, encrypt-then-MAC, compression Not implemented. Only null compression is accepted TLS 1.3, QUIC, ECH Not implemented

docs.title: Development
docs.text: How to build, check and change the library. Contribution rules are in CONTRIBUTING.md.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go at the version go.mod declares. Every Make target except upstream-check runs with exactly that toolchain, which Go downloads on first use when the installed version differs.
  • A C compiler, make, perl and curl for make test-interop, which downloads and builds OpenSSL 1.1.1w.
  • Python 3 with the pinned MkDocs dependencies for the documentation site, installed by make docs-deps. CI uses Python 3.13.

Linters and other tools are downloaded into bin/ at pinned versions by the Make targets that need them.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text: Path Content root package srptls The library. Architecture describes the files example_test.go The package examples, which the documentation site includes scripts/build-openssl.sh Builds the OpenSSL 1.1.1w command line tool for the interop test docs/ This site

docs.title: Common commands
docs.text:
make test           # go vet and the tests under the race detector
make lint           # golangci-lint
make actionlint     # lint the GitHub Actions workflows
make test-interop   # the client against OpenSSL 1.1.1w s_server
make govulncheck    # known vulnerabilities that reach the code
make gitleaks       # leaked credentials in the tree and the history
make docs-build     # strict MkDocs build
make help           # every target

make fmt-check fails when a tracked Go file is not gofmt formatted and make tidy-check when go.mod or go.sum is not tidy. Pull requests to main and dev must pass the tests, lint, the OpenSSL interop test, govulncheck and gitleaks.

docs.title: Following Go releases
docs.text:
Most of the package is crypto/tls from Go 1.27.2. alert.go, cipher_suites.go, common.go, conn.go, handshake_messages.go, handshake_server.go, prf.go and tls.go are the kept files. The Upstream Go workflow runs two checks on every push and pull request to dev and main and weekly:

  • make upstream-check fails when a kept file changed between UPSTREAM_GO_VERSION (1.27.2) and the installed Go release, which CI makes the newest stable release. Set UPSTREAM_CANDIDATE=go1.28.0 to compare with a specific release. When it fails, port the changes that affect the TLS 1.2 client or server, the CBC record layer or the handshake message parsing, then raise UPSTREAM_GO_VERSION in the Makefile to the release you ported.
  • make go-version-check fails when a newer patch release of the Go minor version in go.mod exists. Raise the go directive to that release.

make upstream-check prints the diff. To see it for one file:

git diff --no-index "$(GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.27.2 go env GOROOT)/src/crypto/tls/conn.go" "$(go env GOROOT)/src/crypto/tls/conn.go"

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
The site is built with MkDocs and the Material theme from docs/ and mkdocs.yml. Set PYTHON when the MkDocs toolchain lives in a virtual environment:

make docs-deps PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
make docs-serve PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
  • Go code on the pages comes from example_test.go through named snippet sections, which start and end with --8<-- marker comments. go test compiles every example and runs those with an // Output: comment, so the code on the site cannot drift from the library. Keep the marker comments when you edit the examples.
  • make docs-build runs with --strict, so a broken link, a missing anchor, a missing snippet or a page absent from the navigation fails the build.
  • docs/requirements.txt pins every package by version and SHA-256 hash, including the transitive ones. make docs-deps installs it with --require-hashes. To change a version, edit docs/requirements.in and run make docs-requirements, which needs pip-tools in the PYTHON environment. Dependabot updates the compiled file the same way.

The Documentation workflow runs the same build on every change to the site sources and publishes the site from main to the gh-pages branch. The build runs with a read-only token and hands the site to a separate publish job as an artifact, so the only job that can write to the repository runs no code from PyPI or from the checkout.

Package documentation on pkg.go.dev comes from the Go doc comments. User-facing behavior changes belong in both places.

docs.title: Release process
docs.text:
RELEASE_NOTES.md has one section per version. Run the release check on main, then push a signed version tag:

VERSION=v0.1.0 make release-check
git tag -s v0.1.0 -m 'v0.1.0'
git push origin main v0.1.0

The release check exports HEAD with git archive, builds, vets and tests the export and imports it from a separate module, which catches untracked and local-only files. With VERSION set it also checks that RELEASE_NOTES.md has a section for the version and no Unreleased section.

Pushing a version tag starts the Release workflow. It can also be started by hand for an existing tag. It:

  1. refuses to rebuild a release that is already published,
  2. checks that the tag is reachable from the default branch,
  3. builds the release description from the section of RELEASE_NOTES.md,
  4. repeats the release check on the tag,
  5. generates a CycloneDX SBOM, complete source archives and SHA-256 checksums,
  6. attests the build provenance of the artifacts,
  7. creates a draft release with those assets.

Review the draft and publish it. Do not publish a release from the GitHub UI. Publishing creates the tag, which starts the workflow. The workflow then refuses to rebuild the published release.

The documentation site is not part of a release. It is published from main whenever its sources change.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: make test runs go vet and the tests under the race detector. CI runs it on every push and pull request to dev and main, after checking that the module files are tidy and the code is gofmt formatted.

docs.title: What the tests cover
docs.text:
File Coverage srp_test.go The test vectors of RFC 5054, Appendix B, that every group prime is a safe prime, Verifier.Validate, SimulatedVerifier, NewSalt and the checks on A and B handshake_test.go The server against a minimal test client: handshakes in every group, cipher suite selection, the handshake without Extended Master Secret, refusals and their alerts, renegotiation and plain HTTP on the TLS port handshake_client_test.go The client against Server in every group and cipher suite. The client against a fake server that breaks the protocol on purpose: configuration errors, the ClientHello, SNI, key logs, refusals in both directions, renegotiation and net/http example_test.go The package examples. Example and Example_openSSLVerifierFile run and check their output interop_openssl_test.go The client against OpenSSL 1.1.1w s_server. See Tested implementations

go test -short skips the handshakes in the groups above 3072 bits and the safe prime check of the groups above 2048 bits.

docs.title: Interoperability
docs.text: make test-interop builds OpenSSL 1.1.1w and runs TestOpenSSLServer. Without SRPTLS_TEST_OPENSSL that test is skipped, so make test needs no OpenSSL. The Interoperability workflow runs it on every push and pull request to dev and main and caches the OpenSSL binary, keyed on the hash of scripts/build-openssl.sh.

docs.title: Adding tests
docs.text: A protocol change needs a negative test. A new refusal needs a case in the failure tables of handshake_test.go or handshake_client_test.go that checks the alert and the error each side reports.

docs.title: Channel binding and Extended Master Secret
tls-unique
docs.text:
ConnectionState.TLSUnique holds the tls-unique channel binding of RFC 5929, Section 3: the first Finished message of the handshake. Every handshake here is a full handshake, so that is the client's Finished message, 12 bytes long. The client and the server report the same value.

An EST client that links its certificate request to the TLS connection base64 encodes this value and puts it in the challenge-password attribute of its CSR. The EST server compares it with its own TLSUnique (RFC 7030, Section 3.5). Read the value after the handshake:

state := conn.ConnectionState()
challengePassword := base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(state.TLSUnique)

Before the handshake completes, ConnectionState returns zero values and TLSUnique is empty. The value never changes afterwards, because the connection cannot renegotiate.

docs.title: Extended Master Secret
docs.text:
Extended Master Secret (RFC 7627) derives the master secret from a hash of the handshake messages up to and including the ClientKeyExchange instead of from the client and server random values.

  • The client always offers it.
  • The server uses it whenever the client offers it.
  • The client also completes a handshake with a server that does not use it.

ConnectionState.ExtendedMasterSecret reports whether the connection used it. When your protocol depends on it, check the field after the handshake and close the connection when it is false.

docs.title: Exporting keying material
docs.text:
ConnectionState.ExportKeyingMaterial(label, context, length) derives key material from the connection as RFC 5705 specifies. A nil context is left out of the derivation, which is not the same as an empty one. It returns an error:

  • before the handshake has completed,
  • when the connection did not use Extended Master Secret,
  • when the context is 65536 bytes or longer,
  • for the labels the TLS key schedule reserves: client finished, server finished, master secret, key expansion and extended master secret.

Both sides of a connection export the same bytes for the same label, context and length.

docs.title: Cipher suites
docs.text:
The package implements the three SRP cipher suites of RFC 5054, Section 2.7 that need no server certificate.

Constant ID OpenSSL name Encryption Default TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA 0xC020 SRP-AES-256-CBC-SHA AES-256-CBC First TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA 0xC01D SRP-AES-128-CBC-SHA AES-128-CBC Second TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA 0xC01A SRP-3DES-EDE-CBC-SHA 3DES-EDE-CBC No

All three protect records with CBC and HMAC-SHA1 and use the TLS 1.2 PRF with SHA-256. RFC 5054 defines no AEAD SRP cipher suites. CipherSuiteName returns the standard name of an ID. For an ID the package does not implement it returns a hexadecimal fallback such as 0xC02F.

docs.title: Choosing a suite
docs.text:
Config.CipherSuites is the preference order on both sides. When it is nil, the order is AES-256 and then AES-128, the order of libest and OpenSSL clients. The 3DES suite is used only when it is listed.

Side Rule Server Picks the first suite of its own order that the client offers, whatever the client's order. A ClientHello without a common suite gets a handshake_failure alert Client Offers its order and leaves out IDs the package does not implement. A Config.CipherSuites with none of the three suites fails the handshake before anything is sent

The client refuses a ServerHello that selects a suite it did not offer with an illegal_parameter alert. ConnectionState.CipherSuite reports the suite in use.

To offer or accept 3DES for an old peer, list it after the AES suites:

config.CipherSuites = []uint16{
    srptls.TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA,
    srptls.TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA,
    srptls.TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA,
}

docs.title: Not implemented
docs.text:
• TLS_SRP_SHA_RSA_WITH_* and TLS_SRP_SHA_DSS_WITH_*, which add a server certificate and a signed ServerKeyExchange.
  • Encrypt-then-MAC. The CBC suites use MAC-then-encrypt. The record layer keeps the partial Lucky13 countermeasures of crypto/tls. See the Security model.

docs.title: Connecting as a client
docs.text: The client signs in with a username and a password. It needs no CA certificates: a server that completes the handshake has proved that it holds the verifier of that username and password.

docs.title: Running the handshake
docs.text:
Client wraps a connection you dialed. Config.Username is required. In this code from Example, l is the listener of the server on Getting started:

raw, err := net.DialTimeout("tcp", l.Addr().String(), 10*time.Second)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
conn := srptls.Client(raw, &srptls.Config{
    Username:   "device-1",
    Password:   "secret",
    ServerName: "localhost",
})
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
err = conn.HandshakeContext(ctx)
cancel()
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

greeting, err := bufio.NewReader(conn).ReadString('\n')
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
state := conn.ConnectionState()
fmt.Print(greeting)
fmt.Println(srptls.CipherSuiteName(state.CipherSuite))
fmt.Println("extended master secret:", state.ExtendedMasterSecret)
fmt.Println("tls-unique bytes:", len(state.TLSUnique))
conn.Close()

The handshake runs when you call Handshake or HandshakeContext or on the first Read or Write. Close the connection when the handshake fails.

Field Meaning Username Required, 1 to 255 bytes. Sent in the clear in the ClientHello Password The password the server's verifier was made from ServerName Sent as SNI. A trailing dot is removed and an IP address is not sent MinGroupBits The smallest group accepted. 2048 when zero CipherSuites The cipher suites to offer, in order. See Cipher suites Rand The source of the client random, the SRP exponent and the CBC IVs. crypto/rand when nil KeyLogWriter NSS key log output for debugging

The username and the password are hashed as given. RFC 5054 asks for SASLprep, but the library does not apply it, as OpenSSL does not. Two passwords that look the same but differ in Unicode normalization give different verifiers.

docs.title: Configuration errors
docs.text:
The handshake fails before anything is sent when:

  • the Config is nil,
  • the username is empty or longer than 255 bytes,
  • MinGroupBits is negative or above 8192,
  • CipherSuites lists none of the package's cipher suites.

docs.title: What the client checks
docs.text:
The client fails the handshake and sends an alert when the server:

Server behavior Alert the client sends Selects a version other than TLS 1.2 protocol_version Selects a cipher suite the client did not offer or a compression method other than null illegal_parameter Sends a non-empty renegotiation_info handshake_failure Answers an extension the client did not send unsupported_extension Sends a group that is smaller than MinGroupBits or not in RFC 5054, Appendix A insufficient_security Sends B that is zero modulo N, not below N or gives u = 0 illegal_parameter Sends a Finished message that does not decrypt bad_record_mac Sends a Finished message that decrypts but does not verify handshake_failure

The last two mean that the server does not hold the verifier of this username and password or that the records were altered on the way. The client's error then wraps none of the sentinel errors below, because those stand for alerts the server sent.

When the server refuses the client, the handshake error wraps a sentinel error:

Server alert Client error wraps Meaning bad_record_mac ErrWrongPassword Wrong password or an unknown username the server hides with a simulated verifier unknown_psk_identity ErrUnknownUsername The server says the username does not exist access_denied ErrAccessDenied The server refused the client, for example over a rate limit

RFC 5054, Section 3.3 warns that an attacker on the path can insert an unknown_psk_identity alert, so do not draw conclusions from it alone. Errors and alerts lists every error form.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
The client accepts only the seven groups of RFC 5054 and, by default, only those of 2048 bits and more. Set MinGroupBits to 1024 or 1536 to sign in to a server that still uses a smaller group:

config := &srptls.Config{
    Username:     "device-1",
    Password:     password,
    MinGroupBits: 1024,
}

MinGroupBits is compared with the prime size, so a value between two group sizes accepts the larger groups only.

docs.title: With net/http
docs.text:
Run the handshake in http.Transport.DialTLSContext. net/http fills Response.TLS only for crypto/tls connections, so read the connection state from the Conn instead:

config := &srptls.Config{
    Username:   "device-1",
    Password:   "secret",
    ServerName: "est.example",
}
transport := &http.Transport{
    DialTLSContext: func(ctx context.Context, network, addr string) (net.Conn, error) {
        raw, err := new(net.Dialer).DialContext(ctx, network, addr)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        conn := srptls.Client(raw, config)
        if err := conn.HandshakeContext(ctx); err != nil {
            raw.Close()
            if errors.Is(err, srptls.ErrWrongPassword) {
                return nil, fmt.Errorf("wrong username or password: %w", err)
            }
            return nil, err
        }
        log.Printf("tls-unique %x", conn.ConnectionState().TLSUnique)
        return conn, nil
    },
}
client := &http.Client{Transport: transport, Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
resp, err := client.Get("https://est.example:8443/.well-known/est/cacerts")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
defer resp.Body.Close()

This code is Example_httpClient in example_test.go. The transport dials a new connection with a new handshake whenever it has no idle connection to reuse.

docs.title: Renegotiation
docs.text: The client never renegotiates. A HelloRequest from the server after the handshake is answered with a no_renegotiation warning, the Read that received it returns an error and the connection can no longer be written to.

docs.title: Running a server
docs.text: A TLS-SRP server needs one thing from you: Config.GetVerifier, which returns the stored verifier for the username in the ClientHello. The server needs no certificate and no private key.

docs.title: Accepting connections
docs.text:
Listen opens a listener whose Accept returns *srptls.Conn values. NewListener wraps a listener you already have and Server wraps a single connection:

l, err := srptls.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0", &srptls.Config{
    GetVerifier: func(info *srptls.ClientHelloInfo) (*srptls.Verifier, error) {
        if info.Username == "device-1" {
            return stored, nil
        }
        return nil, srptls.ErrUnknownUsername
    },
})
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

go func() {
    c, err := l.Accept()
    if err != nil {
        return
    }
    defer c.Close()
    // The library sets no handshake deadline.
    c.SetDeadline(time.Now().Add(10 * time.Second))
    conn := c.(*srptls.Conn)
    if err := conn.Handshake(); err != nil {
        log.Print(err)
        return
    }
    fmt.Fprintf(conn, "hello %s\n", conn.ConnectionState().SRPUsername)
}()

Listen returns an error when GetVerifier is not set. NewListener and Server do not check it. A handshake without it fails with an internal_error alert.

The handshake runs when you call Handshake or HandshakeContext or on the first Read or Write. After it completes, ConnectionState().SRPUsername holds the username the client proved it holds the password of. Connection state lists the other fields.

docs.title: The GetVerifier callback
docs.text:
GetVerifier receives a ClientHelloInfo:

Field Content Username The username from the srp extension, as sent. It is 1 to 255 bytes and may not be valid UTF-8 ServerName The host name from the server_name extension. Empty when the client sent none CipherSuites The cipher suites the client offered Conn The underlying connection. Do not read from it or write to it Context() The handshake context, canceled when the handshake ends

It is called once per handshake, after the server has chosen a cipher suite and before any SRP computation. Its return value decides how the handshake continues:

Return Result A verifier The server validates it and continues. An invalid verifier ends the handshake with internal_error ErrUnknownUsername unknown_psk_identity alert. The client learns that the username does not exist ErrAccessDenied, also wrapped access_denied alert Any other error internal_error alert

A ClientHello without the srp extension never reaches GetVerifier. The server answers it with unknown_psk_identity, as RFC 5054, Section 2.5.1.2 recommends.

To hide which usernames exist, return a SimulatedVerifier for unknown ones. To refuse a client before the SRP computation, return ErrAccessDenied. Unknown usernames and refusals covers both.

The server's handshake error is the error GetVerifier returned, so errors.Is finds your own errors too.

docs.title: Deadlines and handshake cost
docs.text:
The library sets no handshake deadline. A client that opens a connection and sends nothing holds it open until you close it. Set a deadline on each accepted connection with SetDeadline before its handshake or run the handshake with HandshakeContext. Canceling the context during the handshake closes the connection.

The handshake is costly for the server. Once GetVerifier returns a verifier, the server computes B, one modular exponentiation, before it reads anything more from the client. A ClientKeyExchange with any value of A makes it compute two more before the client's Finished message shows whether the client knows the password. The cost grows roughly with the square of the group size. Limit the connections a client can open. A reverse proxy in front of the server can enforce both the limit and the deadline. The Security model has the details.

docs.title: With net/http
docs.text:
net/http fills Request.TLS only for crypto/tls connections, so it stays nil here. Save the connection with http.Server.ConnContext and read its ConnectionState in the handler. The handshake runs on the first read, so ReadHeaderTimeout also limits it:

l, err := srptls.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0", config)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
srv := &http.Server{
    // The handshake runs in the first read, so this also bounds it.
    ReadHeaderTimeout: 10 * time.Second,
    ConnContext: func(ctx context.Context, c net.Conn) context.Context {
        return context.WithValue(ctx, connKey{}, c)
    },
    Handler: http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        state := r.Context().Value(connKey{}).(*srptls.Conn).ConnectionState()
        fmt.Fprintf(w, "hello %s\n", state.SRPUsername)
    }),
}
go srv.Serve(l)
defer srv.Close()

This code is Example_httpServer in example_test.go. The config it uses answers unknown usernames with a simulated verifier, as shown on Unknown usernames and refusals.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: Config.KeyLogWriter writes the master secret of every handshake in the NSS key log format, which Wireshark reads to decrypt a capture. Anyone with the log can decrypt the connections, so use it only for debugging.

docs.title: Unknown usernames and refusals
docs.text:
GetVerifier decides what a client with an unknown username learns and whether a client is refused before the SRP computation.

GetVerifier returns Alert Client error wraps The client learns SimulatedVerifier(...) bad_record_mac ErrWrongPassword Nothing. It looks like a wrong password ErrUnknownUsername unknown_psk_identity ErrUnknownUsername The username does not exist ErrAccessDenied, also wrapped access_denied ErrAccessDenied It was refused

The first two rows follow RFC 5054, Section 2.5.1.3, which lets a server either reveal an unknown username or simulate a verifier for it.

docs.title: Simulated verifiers
docs.text:
SimulatedVerifier(seed, group, username) returns a verifier for a username the server does not know. The handshake then runs to the end and fails like a wrong password, so the client cannot tell whether the username exists:

// The seed is a secret. Generate at least 16 random bytes once, store them
// with the verifiers and use the same value on every instance and across
// restarts.
seed, err := hex.DecodeString(os.Getenv("SRP_SIMULATED_SEED"))
if err != nil || len(seed) < 16 {
    log.Fatal("SRP_SIMULATED_SEED must hold at least 32 hexadecimal digits")
}

config := &srptls.Config{
    GetVerifier: func(info *srptls.ClientHelloInfo) (*srptls.Verifier, error) {
        if info.Username == "device-1" {
            return stored, nil
        }
        return srptls.SimulatedVerifier(seed, group, []byte(info.Username)), nil
    },
}

This is part of Example_httpServer in example_test.go, which reads the seed from the SRP_SIMULATED_SEED environment variable.

The salt and the value are derived from the seed and the username with HMAC, so the same seed and username always give the same salt. The salt is 20 bytes and never starts with a zero byte, like a salt from NewSalt. The value is a pseudo-random number below N rather than g^x. Computing it needs no modular exponentiation. Once GetVerifier returns, the handshake costs the server the same work as with a real verifier. How long your own lookup takes before it returns is up to you.

The simulation holds only when the inputs stay fixed:

  • The seed is a secret key. Generate at least 16 random bytes once and store them with the verifiers. Anyone who knows the seed can compute the salt of any unknown username and so tell unknown usernames from real ones.
  • Use the same seed everywhere. A seed that differs between server instances or changes on a restart makes the salt of an unknown username change, which a real user's salt never does.
  • Use the group of the stored verifiers. The server sends the group in the clear, so an unknown username answered in another group stands out. If your stored verifiers use more than one group, every unknown username still gets the one group you pass.

docs.title: Revealing unknown usernames
docs.text:
Returning ErrUnknownUsername sends an unknown_psk_identity alert and saves the server the SRP computation. The client error wraps ErrUnknownUsername. Use it when usernames are not secret.

A ClientHello without the srp extension gets the same alert, without a call to GetVerifier.

docs.title: Refusing a client
docs.text:
Return ErrAccessDenied or an error that wraps it to refuse a client before the server does any SRP computation. The server sends an access_denied alert and its handshake error is the error you returned:

GetVerifier: func(info *srptls.ClientHelloInfo) (*srptls.Verifier, error) {
    if limiter.blocked(info.Username) {
        return nil, fmt.Errorf("too many failed sign-ins for %q: %w", info.Username, srptls.ErrAccessDenied)
    }
    return lookup(info.Username)
},

docs.title: Limiting password guessing
docs.text:
Every handshake lets a client test one password guess, so an online attacker can keep trying. RFC 5054, Section 3.3 asks servers to limit the rate of attempts per address or per username. The library provides the two hooks. The counting is yours:

  1. Count a failed sign-in when the server's handshake error wraps ErrWrongPassword. A wrong password and an unknown username answered with a simulated verifier both do.
  2. Check the count in GetVerifier and return ErrAccessDenied once it is used up.

ClientHelloInfo.Username and ClientHelloInfo.Conn.RemoteAddr() identify the user and the address. An attacker who alters the client's records on the way also causes ErrWrongPassword, so a counter per username lets an attacker on the path lock that user out.

docs.title: What a verifier is
docs.text:
A Verifier is the stored SRP record of one username:

Field Content Group One of the seven RFC 5054 groups Salt 1 to 255 bytes, sent to the client exactly as stored Value v = g^x mod N in big-endian bytes, with or without leading zeros

NewVerifier computes it as RFC 5054, Section 2.4 specifies: x = SHA1(s | SHA1(I | ":" | P)) and v = g^x mod N. The username I and the password P are hashed as given, without SASLprep, as OpenSSL does.

The server needs no password. A verifier is still sensitive: whoever reads it can test password guesses offline and can pose as the server to that user (RFC 5054, Section 3.3). Protect stored verifiers like password hashes.

docs.title: Creating a verifier
docs.text:
group, err := srptls.GroupByBits(3072)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
salt, err := srptls.NewSalt(rand.Reader)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
stored, err := srptls.NewVerifier(group, []byte("device-1"), []byte("secret"), salt)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

NewSalt returns 20 random bytes whose first byte is not zero. OpenSSL clients read the salt as a number and drop leading zero bytes, so a salt that starts with zero would give them another x and the handshake would fail like a wrong password. NewVerifier accepts any salt of 1 to 255 bytes, so use NewSalt unless you have a reason not to. The username must be 1 to 255 bytes.

docs.title: Storing and loading verifiers
docs.text:
Store the username, the group size, the salt and the value. To load a record, look the group up with GroupByBits and fill in the fields:

group, err := srptls.GroupByBits(record.GroupBits)
if err != nil {
    return nil, err
}
v := &srptls.Verifier{Group: group, Salt: record.Salt, Value: record.Value}
if err := v.Validate(); err != nil {
    return nil, err
}

Validate checks that the verifier has an RFC 5054 group, a salt of 1 to 255 bytes and a value that is not zero and is below N. The server runs the same check on every verifier GetVerifier returns and ends the handshake with an internal_error alert when it fails. Calling Validate when you load a record finds a damaged record earlier, with a clearer error.

The verifier only works with the group it was made in. Changing a user's group or password means creating a new verifier from the password.

docs.title: Groups
docs.text:
The package has the seven groups of RFC 5054, Appendix A and no way to define another, because OpenSSL clients accept only these.

Prime size in bits Generator 1024 2 1536 2 2048 2 3072 5 4096 5 6144 5 8192 19
  • GroupByBits returns the group with a prime of the given size.
  • GroupByParameters returns the group whose prime and generator match the given big-endian bytes. Leading zero bytes are ignored.
  • Group.Bits, Group.N and Group.Generator return the size, a copy of the prime and a copy of the generator.

The server sends the group of each user's verifier. The client accepts 2048 bits and more unless its MinGroupBits allows the smaller groups. A larger group costs both sides more per handshake, roughly with the square of the prime size.

docs.title: Importing OpenSSL verifier files
docs.text:
openssl srp stores users in a text file, the srpvfile, that openssl s_server -srpvfile reads. Each user is one line of tab-separated fields: the entry type, the verifier, the salt, the username, the group and an info field. Only lines of type V hold valid users.

The verifier and the salt are numbers written in OpenSSL's own base 64 alphabet, not standard base 64. For the groups OpenSSL ships, the group field is the prime size in bits. This code reads one line, decodes both numbers to big-endian bytes without leading zeros and builds a Verifier:

// openssl srp -srpvfile srpvfile -add -gn 2048 -passout pass:secret device-1
// wrote this line. Its fields are separated by tabs: the entry type, the
// verifier, the salt, the username, the group and an info field.
line := "" +
    "V\t" +
    "09XhP7Rygmz11SS0DG4K5xiZG1ZQd9EWGKrcj8hrTflO.jHVanjs8pty5i75DwZL" +
    "0S4WoSFE/MHquQvcDR3k6mdrPw4ICmL.7BAwSY2IZNbnq6DwO0Z0iKDNjtJVX00K" +
    "GXD/i/CbNXN/DLRdGksYUPp8y3B4XWmxGYls38r1bkXMcX0kKeVO8hJGV/lO0vvc" +
    "p2Fw8iap2MtiDX0vFRUE7WX2MtU9TyHM.z1Pc8Z894v9H2l1oKw5YcbXAce2OsCJ" +
    "T5YmQU3FQo5KJeYuvOfmZAer0Ur24rHfUzC9Fie3tJQ1STQ84j2J1CMvbfO5biZf" +
    "rPy6azssYuu6VtcIfoZ1Ae\t" +
    "8RgioHW1582bhjJhyBvFIRK4Up7\tdevice-1\t2048\t"

// OpenSSL writes the verifier and the salt as numbers in its own base 64
// alphabet, without padding and without leading zero digits.
const alphabet = "0123456789ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz./"
decode := func(s string) ([]byte, error) {
    n := new(big.Int)
    for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ {
        digit := strings.IndexByte(alphabet, s[i])
        if digit < 0 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("invalid character %q", s[i])
        }
        n.Lsh(n, 6).Or(n, big.NewInt(int64(digit)))
    }
    // Bytes drops leading zero bytes, as OpenSSL does with the salt.
    return n.Bytes(), nil
}

fields := strings.Split(line, "\t")
if len(fields) != 6 || fields[0] != "V" {
    log.Fatal("not the entry of a valid user")
}
value, err := decode(fields[1])
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
salt, err := decode(fields[2])
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
// For the groups OpenSSL ships, the group field is the prime size in bits.
bits, err := strconv.Atoi(fields[4])
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
group, err := srptls.GroupByBits(bits)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
username := fields[3]
stored := &srptls.Verifier{Group: group, Salt: salt, Value: value}
if err := stored.Validate(); err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}

It is Example_openSSLVerifierFile in example_test.go, which signs in with the password the line was made from. Dropping leading zero bytes from the salt matters: OpenSSL computes x from the salt as a number, so a salt imported with a leading zero byte would fail like a wrong password.

docs.title: OpenSSL s_server
docs.text:
The Interoperability workflow runs the client against openssl s_server from OpenSSL 1.1.1w on every push and pull request to dev and main. The test is TestOpenSSLServer in interop_openssl_test.go.

Item Value Peer openssl s_server from OpenSSL 1.1.1w, built from the source release by scripts/build-openssl.sh with a pinned SHA-256 checksum Verifiers Made by openssl srp in an srpvfile, one user per group Runner ubuntu-latest with the Go version from go.mod

The test runs these cases:

Case Group Cipher suite Expected result Sign-in 2048 AES-256 Handshake succeeds Sign-in 3072 AES-128 Handshake succeeds Sign-in 4096 AES-256 Handshake succeeds Sign-in 8192 AES-256 Handshake succeeds Small group allowed 1024, with MinGroupBits 1024 AES-256 Handshake succeeds Small group refused 1024, default MinGroupBits AES-256 The client refuses the group Wrong password 2048 AES-256 The client error wraps ErrWrongPassword Unknown username None AES-256 The client error wraps ErrUnknownUsername

For each successful handshake the test checks that:

  • the connection uses TLS 1.2, the requested cipher suite and Extended Master Secret,
  • s_server reports the same cipher suite under its OpenSSL name,
  • application data passes in both directions,
  • ExportKeyingMaterial returns the same 32 bytes that s_server exports with -keymatexport,
  • the master secret in the client's key log appears in the key log of s_server.

The 1536 and 6144 bit groups and the 3DES cipher suite are not part of this test. No test runs an OpenSSL client against the package's server.

docs.title: Running the test
docs.text:
make test-interop

This builds OpenSSL 1.1.1w under bin/openssl-1.1.1 on first use and runs TestOpenSSLServer. The build needs a C compiler, make, perl and curl. To test with another OpenSSL 1.1.1 binary, point SRPTLS_TEST_OPENSSL at it:

SRPTLS_TEST_OPENSSL=/path/to/openssl go test -run TestOpenSSLServer -v .

Without SRPTLS_TEST_OPENSSL the test is skipped, so make test does not need OpenSSL.

docs.title: OpenSSL 3.0 and later
docs.text:
The test uses OpenSSL 1.1.1 because, as its comment records, openssl s_server from OpenSSL 3.0.22, 3.5.9, 3.6.5 and 4.0.3 closes the connection during its SRP user lookup, also with its own s_client.

openssl s_client from OpenSSL 3.0 onward has a bug in its -srpuser handling that discards the -srppass password and signs in with an empty one (openssl/openssl#32565). The handshake then fails like a wrong password. Test a server with OpenSSL 1.1.1 s_client or with a program that calls the libssl SRP functions directly.

docs.title: Config
docs.text:
One Config type serves both sides. Some fields apply to one side only. Do not change a Config after passing it to a function of the package. A Config may be reused for many connections.

Field Side Default Rules GetVerifier func(*ClientHelloInfo) (*Verifier, error) Server None, required See Running a server Username string Client None, required 1 to 255 bytes, hashed as given without SASLprep Password string Client Empty Hashed as given without SASLprep ServerName string Client Empty, no SNI A trailing dot is removed. An IP address is not sent MinGroupBits int Client 2048 when zero 0 to 8192. Groups with a smaller prime are refused CipherSuites []uint16 Both AES-256, then AES-128 when nil The preference order. See Cipher suites Rand io.Reader Both crypto/rand when nil Source of the random values and the SRP exponents KeyLogWriter io.Writer Both None Receives the master secrets in NSS key log format. For debugging only

A client Config that breaks these rules fails the handshake before anything is sent. Server and NewListener need a non-nil Config. The server handshake checks only that GetVerifier is set.

docs.title: ClientHelloInfo
docs.text:
The argument of GetVerifier.

Field or method Content Username string The SRP username, as sent. 1 to 255 bytes, possibly not valid UTF-8 ServerName string The SNI host name. Empty when the client sent none CipherSuites []uint16 The cipher suites the client offered Conn net.Conn The underlying connection. Reading from it or writing to it breaks the handshake Context() context.Context A child of the context passed to HandshakeContext, canceled when the handshake ends

docs.title: Constructors
docs.text: Function Returns Client(conn net.Conn, config *Config) *Conn A client connection over conn Server(conn net.Conn, config *Config) *Conn A server connection over conn Listen(network, laddr string, config *Config) (net.Listener, error) A listener from net.Listen whose connections are *Conn. Fails when GetVerifier is not set NewListener(inner net.Listener, config *Config) net.Listener inner with each accepted connection wrapped in Server

docs.title: Verifiers and groups
docs.text:
Function or method Purpose NewVerifier(group *Group, username, password, salt []byte) (*Verifier, error) Computes a verifier. The username must be 1 to 255 bytes NewSalt(rand io.Reader) ([]byte, error) 20 random bytes whose first byte is not zero SimulatedVerifier(seed []byte, group *Group, username []byte) *Verifier A stable fake verifier for an unknown username (*Verifier).Validate() error Checks the group, a salt of 1 to 255 bytes and a value that is not zero and below N GroupByBits(bits int) (*Group, error) The RFC 5054 group of that prime size GroupByParameters(n, g []byte) (*Group, error) The RFC 5054 group with that prime and generator (*Group).Bits() int, N() []byte, Generator() []byte The prime size and copies of the prime and the generator

Verifiers and groups explains how to use them.

docs.title: ConnectionState
docs.text:
Conn.ConnectionState() describes a connection. Until the handshake has completed, every field except HandshakeComplete is zero.

Field or method Content Version uint16 Always VersionTLS12 HandshakeComplete bool Whether the handshake has completed CipherSuite uint16 The cipher suite in use, such as TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA ServerName string The SNI host name the client sent. On the client it is empty when Config.ServerName is empty or an IP address SRPUsername string The username the client proved it holds the password of. On the client it is Config.Username ExtendedMasterSecret bool Whether the connection used Extended Master Secret TLSUnique []byte The tls-unique channel binding, the client's 12-byte Finished message ExportKeyingMaterial(label string, context []byte, length int) ([]byte, error) RFC 5705 key material. Needs Extended Master Secret

Channel binding and Extended Master Secret explains the last three.

docs.title: Conn
docs.text:
*Conn implements net.Conn.

Method Behavior Handshake() error Runs the handshake if it has not run. After a failure every call returns the stored error HandshakeContext(ctx context.Context) error Like Handshake. Canceling ctx during the handshake closes the connection and returns the context error. Later calls return the error of the closed connection. Once the handshake has completed, the context has no effect Read(b []byte) (int, error) and Write(b []byte) (int, error) Run the handshake first if needed Close() error Sends a close_notify alert when the handshake has completed and closes the connection CloseWrite() error Sends close_notify without closing the underlying connection. Fails before the handshake has completed SetDeadline, SetReadDeadline and SetWriteDeadline Set the deadlines of the underlying connection. After a write times out, every later write fails NetConn() net.Conn The underlying connection. Reading from it or writing to it corrupts the TLS connection LocalAddr() and RemoteAddr() The addresses of the underlying connection

Read and Write call Handshake, so set a deadline for both before the first call when the handshake has not run yet. Otherwise a silent peer blocks them indefinitely.

docs.title: Constants
docs.text:
Constant Value VersionTLS10 0x0301 VersionTLS11 0x0302 VersionTLS12 0x0303 TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA 0xC01A TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA 0xC01D TLS_SRP_SHA_WITH_AES_256_CBC_SHA 0xC020

CipherSuiteName(id uint16) string returns the name of a cipher suite ID.

docs.title: Sentinel errors
docs.text:
Test handshake errors with errors.Is.

Error On the server On the client ErrWrongPassword Wrapped by the handshake error when the client's Finished message does not decrypt or does not verify. A wrong password or a simulated verifier causes it. So does a client whose records were altered on the way Wrapped by the handshake error when the server sends bad_record_mac ErrUnknownUsername Return it from GetVerifier to send unknown_psk_identity. The handshake error is the returned error Wrapped by the handshake error when the server sends unknown_psk_identity ErrAccessDenied Return it or an error that wraps it from GetVerifier to send access_denied. The handshake error is the returned error Wrapped by the handshake error when the server sends access_denied

The common outcomes side by side:

Cause Server error Alert to the client Client error wraps Wrong password or an unknown username with a SimulatedVerifier Wraps ErrWrongPassword bad_record_mac ErrWrongPassword GetVerifier returns ErrUnknownUsername The error from GetVerifier unknown_psk_identity ErrUnknownUsername GetVerifier returns ErrAccessDenied The error from GetVerifier access_denied ErrAccessDenied

docs.title: Alerts
docs.text:
An alert received from the peer is a *net.OpError in the error, with Op set to "remote error". The error text names the alert, for example remote error: tls: bad record MAC. An alert this side sent appears as a *net.OpError with Op set to "local error" only when the record layer or the message parser sent it, as with bad_record_mac and decode_error. The other checks return their own error, which describes the cause.

Alerts the server sends:

Alert Cause protocol_version The ClientHello version is below TLS 1.2 illegal_parameter A is zero modulo N, not below N or gives u = 0. Also a ClientHello without null compression handshake_failure No common cipher suite, a non-empty renegotiation_info in the ClientHello or a client Finished message that decrypts but does not verify unknown_psk_identity No srp extension or GetVerifier returned ErrUnknownUsername access_denied GetVerifier returned ErrAccessDenied internal_error GetVerifier is not set, returned another error or returned an invalid verifier bad_record_mac A record does not decrypt. In the handshake this means a wrong password decode_error A malformed handshake message, including a repeated extension or an SNI name with a trailing dot unexpected_message A handshake message out of order, including any handshake message after the handshake

The client sends the alerts listed on Connecting as a client. It also sends decode_error for a malformed message, unexpected_message for a message out of order and a no_renegotiation warning for a HelloRequest after the handshake.

docs.title: Other errors
docs.text:
• Configuration errors. A client Config without a usable username, MinGroupBits or cipher suite fails the handshake before anything is sent. Listen fails without GetVerifier.
  • RecordHeaderError. The peer sent something that is not a TLS record, such as plain HTTP on the TLS port. Its RecordHeader holds the five bytes read. Conn holds the underlying connection when the bytes arrived in place of the first handshake message. It is nil after a handshake or after an alert was sent.
  • Context errors. When the context passed to HandshakeContext is canceled during the handshake, the connection is closed and the context's error is returned.

Every handshake error is kept. Later calls to Handshake, Read and Write on the same Conn return it again. After a canceled HandshakeContext the kept error is the one from the closed connection, not the context error.

docs.title: What the handshake proves
docs.text:
A completed handshake proves to the server that the client knows the password the stored verifier was made from. It proves to the client that the server holds that verifier. Neither side sends the password or the verifier. No certificate is involved. Both proofs are the Finished messages: with a wrong password or without the verifier, the two sides derive different keys and the handshake fails (RFC 5054, Section 2.6).

The username is not protected. The client sends it in the clear in the ClientHello (RFC 5054, Section 3.3), so anyone on the path can read it.

docs.title: What the library checks
docs.text:
• Groups. Both sides use only the seven groups of RFC 5054, Appendix A. The client refuses any other prime or generator and, by default, the 1024 and 1536 bit groups, with an insufficient_security alert.
  • Public values. RFC 5054 requires both sides to refuse a public value that is zero modulo N and calls these checks crucial in Section 3.1. The server refuses such an A and the client such a B with an illegal_parameter alert. Both also refuse values that are not below N or that give u = 0.
  • Exponents. The secret exponents a and b are 384 bits drawn from Config.Rand, above the 256 bits RFC 5054 asks for.
  • Constant-time arithmetic. The modular arithmetic uses filippo.io/bigmod. The client computes (B - k*g^x)^(a + u*x) as base^a * (base^u)^x, so the secrets a and x stay in constant-time exponentiations and their sum is never formed.
  • Finished messages. Both sides compare the Finished message in constant time.
  • Protocol. Only TLS 1.2, no renegotiation, no session resumption and no compression.

docs.title: What RFC 5054 prescribes
docs.text: SRP in TLS uses SHA-1 for the SRP values x, u and k. The cipher suites protect records with CBC and HMAC-SHA1. RFC 5054, Section 3.4 explains why attacks on the collision resistance of SHA-1 do not affect these uses. The CBC record layer keeps the Lucky13 countermeasures of crypto/tls, which are partial: they apply only to the SHA-1 based MACs, which are the only MACs here.

docs.title: What the caller must do
docs.text:
• Protect the verifiers. Whoever reads a verifier can test password guesses offline and can pose as the server to that user (RFC 5054, Section 3.3).
  • Limit password guessing. Every handshake tests one guess. Count failures and refuse clients over the limit, as Limiting password guessing describes.
  • Keep the simulated verifier seed secret and stable. See Simulated verifiers.
  • Bound the handshake. See Denial of service.
  • Keep KeyLogWriter off in production. The key log decrypts every connection it covers.
  • Choose passwords that resist offline guessing. There is no tunable work factor: testing a guess against a stolen verifier costs two SHA-1 hashes and one modular exponentiation.

docs.title: Denial of service
docs.text:
The library sets no handshake deadline and no connection limit. A client that connects and sends nothing keeps the connection open until the caller closes it.

The handshake is costly for the server. The client can make it do most of the work before proving anything:

  1. A single ClientHello makes the server call GetVerifier and, when it returns a verifier, compute B with one modular exponentiation.
  2. A ClientKeyExchange with any value of A makes the server compute two more exponentiations for the premaster secret.
  3. Only then does the client's Finished message show whether it knows the password.

The exponents have fixed lengths, so the cost grows roughly with the square of the group size. A simulated verifier costs the same as a real one. Set a deadline on every accepted connection before its handshake with SetDeadline or HandshakeContext. Limit the connections a client can open. A reverse proxy in front of the server can enforce both. Returning ErrAccessDenied from GetVerifier refuses a client before step 1's exponentiation.

docs.title: Fixes from Go
docs.text: Most of the code is a copy of crypto/tls. A CI job that runs on every push and pull request to dev and main and weekly compares the copied files with the newest Go release and fails when Go changed one of them, so fixes to Go's TLS code are ported. Development describes the process and the security policy how such fixes are rated and released.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Report vulnerabilities privately through GitHub security advisories. The security policy describes the process and the fix targets.
